title: A Better Kind of Classroom
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 36 of 40
content:
The Board accepted Severus's counterproposal with three amendments, two conditions, and one sentence so pompous that he read it aloud in Minerva's office purely so he could sneer at the punctuation.

Minerva had attached a second sheet beneath the appointment terms. It was less ornate and considerably more important: a procedure for students to report unsafe teaching without first confronting the teacher who had frightened them.

Severus read it without comment.

“You object?” Minerva asked.

“I object to its implication that the Headmistress intends to devote an afternoon to explaining what a complaint is.”

“The afternoon is already on your schedule.”

“Efficient.”

She regarded him over her spectacles. “A pupil once had to decide whether it was safer to endure you or report you. I will not build a school in which that is still a reasonable question.”

The words landed. Severus folded the sheet once, precisely, and set it beside the contract.

“I have not asked you to forget it,” he said.

“No,” Minerva replied. “But you have occasionally behaved as though I should.”

I felt the old instinct to intervene, to make the room kinder for a man I loved. It would have been a mistake. They were two adults discussing a school full of children whose safety mattered more than my discomfort.

Severus turned back to the document.

“Add a specified response window and an external reviewer when the complaint names the Head of House. Otherwise the process is theatrical.”

Minerva picked up her quill. “Now that is a useful objection.”

He didn't smile. Later he would, privately, over the ridiculous wording of the Board's other amendments. For now he helped make the rules better and accepted that this was part of being allowed to teach again.

“‘In recognition of exceptional wartime service and with due consideration given to pedagogical concerns arising during prior appointments,’” he quoted, each word sharpened until the phrase sounded like something that ought to be bottled and labeled corrosive. “They have managed to say, in twenty-one words, that I was useful and unpleasant.”

Minerva did not look up from the parchment she was signing. “Both of which are demonstrably true.”

I covered my mouth with one hand.

Severus turned his head toward me. “Your loyalty is moving.”

“I am loyal to accurate summaries.”

“Then you and the Board have much in common.”

Minerva's quill stopped. The corner of her mouth twitched. “If the pair of you are finished courting over administrative language, we might discuss the actual appointment.”

Severus went absolutely still.

I made a choking sound.

Minerva looked serenely innocent.

It was the first time I had ever seen Severus Snape lose an argument before it had properly begun.

He recovered, of course. He always recovered. His mouth compressed, his eyes narrowed, and he sat straighter in the chair. “Advanced N.E.W.T. seminar. Two afternoons per week. Research access by appointment. No Head of House responsibilities. No disciplinary authority outside my classroom except in immediate matters of safety.”

“Correct.”

“Observed lessons.”

“For every returning member of staff during the first term,” Minerva said. “Not merely you.”

His eyes flicked toward her.

That mattered. I could tell by the slight easing of his shoulders.

“Written student complaints routed through the Deputy Headmistress,” she continued. “Again, school-wide. We should have had something of the sort years ago.”

Severus looked down at the parchment. “Yes.”

No sarcasm. No defense. Just yes.

I had learned to recognize how much work could live inside one syllable.

The first class was a week later.

He pretended not to care that I was there.

I pretended to believe him.

The dungeon classroom had changed since the war. The broken shelves were repaired. The jars of preserved things that had once made the room feel like the inside of a threat had been reduced to what was genuinely useful for instruction. New lamps threw clean pools of light over every worktable. A charmed ventilation system hummed softly along the stone ceiling.

Severus inspected it all before the students arrived as if the castle had personally conspired to embarrass him with adequate safety standards.

“You are hovering,” he said without turning.

“I am standing.”

“Near me.”

“That is generally how being in the same room works.”

His hand paused over a stack of parchment. “You have become intolerable.”

“Terrible influence.”

That earned me a glance.

It was not a smile. Severus did not waste perfectly serviceable expressions by giving them names they had not earned. But something warm moved through his eyes before he looked away.

Eight students entered at precisely two o'clock.

Every one of them went quiet when they saw him.

The silence was not respect. Not entirely. Some of it was fear. Some curiosity. Some the uncomfortable fascination reserved for people whose names had appeared in newspapers too often. One Ravenclaw boy stared openly at the scar crossing Severus's throat until a Hufflepuff girl elbowed him.

Severus noticed. Of course he noticed.

He did not punish either of them.

“Sit,” he said.

They sat.

I took a chair along the back wall beside Professor Sinistra, who was observing for the week. Severus had objected to my presence until I reminded him that I had audited three of his laboratory procedures, survived one experimental vapor exposure, and knew exactly how often he cheated by pretending he did not need rest.

He had called that argument irrelevant.

Then he had told me where to sit.

The blackboard filled itself in his narrow handwriting.

ADVANCED ANTIDOTE DESIGN: PRINCIPLES OF UNKNOWN TOXINS.

There were no introductions. No speech about the war. No demand for absolution.

He placed six unlabeled vials on the demonstration table.

“One contains a harmless saline solution,” he said. “One contains an irritant. Four contain compounds designed to imitate common diagnostic signatures without producing the expected underlying effect. You will not taste them, touch them, sniff them, or attempt whatever inspired act of idiocy is currently forming behind Mr. Bell's eyes.”

The Ravenclaw boy's hand froze halfway toward his goggles.

A few students laughed.

Severus's mouth almost moved.

“Your task is not to identify the substances. Your task is to tell me what you would need to know before attempting to identify them.”

A Slytherin girl raised her hand cautiously. “Symptoms?”

“Useful.”

“Time since exposure?” another offered.

“Essential.”

“Known allergies?”

“Better.”

The answers came faster.

Severus moved among the tables, robes brushing the floor. He was still intimidating. He was still exacting. When one student gave a lazy answer, he dismantled it in three sentences so precise that I winced in sympathy.

But he did not humiliate the boy.

That difference would have been invisible to anyone who did not know him.

I knew him.

Halfway through the exercise, a Gryffindor girl misread a reagent chart and reached for the wrong neutralizer. Severus caught her wrist before she touched it.

She flinched.

He released her immediately.

“Miss Patel,” he said, quieter than before, “look again.”

Her face had gone pale.

She looked.

Her eyes widened. “That would react with the aconite marker.”

“Yes.”

“I could have—”

“You did not.”

His voice remained flat, but I saw his fingers flex once at his side. “Why?”

She swallowed. “Because you stopped me.”

“No.” His gaze moved to the chart. “Because the error was detectable. Safety is not the absence of mistakes. It is the construction of enough barriers that one mistake does not become a catastrophe. Correct your notes.”

She did.

No points lost. No cutting remark about incompetence. No public spectacle.

Professor Sinistra wrote something on her observation form.

Severus noticed that too.

After class, when the students had gone, he stood at his desk pretending to reorganize quills that were already aligned.

“Well?” he asked.

“Do you want my answer or the one you can argue with?”

“The distinction has never prevented you from providing both.”

I came closer.

“You were good.”

His expression shuttered.

“Don't.”

“I didn't say perfect.”

The shutters paused.

“You scared Bell half to death over an unlabelled vial.”

“He was about to adjust his goggles.”

“You didn't know that.”

“I knew it in my bones.”

I laughed. “You were still you.”

Something in him eased.

That, I realized, was what he had been afraid of.

Not merely failing.

Becoming so careful that there was nothing left of him except apology.

I leaned against the front table. “You can be sharp without using people as whetstones.”

His eyes lifted to mine.

For several seconds he said nothing.

Then, very softly, “An appalling metaphor.”

“You understood it.”

“Unfortunately.”

He gathered the student parchments. One had been left crooked. He straightened it automatically.

“Patel flinched,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I saw.”

“I know.”

His thumb moved along the paper's edge. “There was a time when I would have interpreted that as proof of control.”

I waited.

He did not need me to rescue him from the sentence.

“At the time,” he continued, “I called fear discipline because it was convenient.”

The room felt suddenly larger and much quieter.

“You can't change those classes,” I said.

“No.”

“You can change this one.”

His gaze moved around the dungeon: new lamps, clean air, unthreatening shelves, eight workstations that would fill again next Tuesday.

“Apparently,” he said, “I have agreed to try.”

I reached for his hand.

He looked down before letting me take it. Consent had become ordinary between us, which made it feel more intimate rather than less.

His fingers closed around mine.

“You know,” I said, “Minerva was right.”

“That sentence has caused generations of suffering.”

“About us courting over administrative language.”

He stared at me.

I smiled sweetly.

“Leave my classroom.”

“You're holding my hand.”

He looked down at our joined fingers as though they had betrayed him.

Then he tightened his grip.

“Detention,” he murmured.

“You don't have disciplinary authority outside immediate safety matters.”

His eyes narrowed.

I had never enjoyed policy so much in my life.
